titleFa: کتاب Academic Writing for Graduate Students
author: John M. Swales & Christine B. Feak
introFa: کتاب «Academic Writing for Graduate Students» نوشته John M. Swales & Christine B. Feak یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Academic Writing for Graduate Students»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

Printed in the USA Reviews ACADEMIC WRITING FOR GRADUATE STUDENTS: A COURSE FOR NONNATIVE SPEAKERS OF ENGLISH. 253pp. ACADEMIC WRITING FOR GRADUATE STUDENTS: COMMEN- TARY. John M. Swales & Christine B. Feak. Ann Arbor: The University of Michigan Press, 1994, 117 pp. Reviewed by L~'ane D. Belcher A number of second language writing specialists see academic discourse in accommodationist and resistance terms, as not just difficult to teach, because of its dizzying variability across the disciplines, but not worth teaching, because of its homogenizing effect on individual difference. Such writing specialists will probably not be attracted to John Swales and Christine Feak's new textbook for advanced nonnative-speaker writers. Much more appreciative, in all likeli- hood, will be the growing number of ESL teachers of graduate students (see Silva, Reichelt, & Lax-Farr 1994), students already committed to learning to write as professionals, and perhaps to changing the world, or some portion of it. While Weissberg and Buker's Writing Up Research. Experimental Research Report Writing for Students of English (1990) has admirably met many of the needs of students and teachers of the research report, and is still, arguably, unsurpassed in the fullness of its pedagogical coverage of this genre, Swales and Feak's Academic Writing for Graduate Students (hereafter A WG) and its companion Commentary provide a wider and much better balanced view of academic writing. This is a perspective that should prove very attractive and useful to teachers of cross-disciplinary groups of graduate students, and to the students themselves, since it provides coverage of the broad range of genres one must "control" to participate fully in an academic discourse community. Even more appealing may be the guidance and incentive that Swales and Feak offer their readers to continue to deepen their knowledge of academic writing on their own. Given A WG's considerable strengths, it is surprising that its initial chapter does not provide more of the guidance and incentive which is so evident in the rest of the text. While Chapter 1 does begin by focusing on "macro" rather than "micro" concerns--that is, with audience and purpose considerations rather than textual features--the "style" and "flow" of academic texts receive the greatest share of Swales and Feak's attention. Of course, as the authors note, new international graduate students are "bombarded" with "mixed messages" regarding academic discourse, and no doubt are in need of explicit help in sorting out registers. Nevertheless, defining academic discourse largely in terms 175

1 7 6 Reviews of "vocabulary shift" toward greater formality, "the most salient feature of academic writing" according to Swales and Feak (AWG: 15), seems rather reductive. Why not begin with a more intellectually compelling social epistemic perspective such as MacDonald's (1994) view of academic writing "as a vehicle for constructing knowledge claims...and taking us out of the ephemerality of individual instances so that we can learn something about our past and our present, while attempting to control or improve our present" (p. 9)? Consider also the "rhetoric of inquiry" approach of Kirscht, Levine, and Reiff (1994), who view the conventions of academic discourse as "tools [that can be] used consciously to aid students in moving beyond the boundaries of previous brief systems and in exploring new perceptions" (p. 374). In fact, beyond its initial chapter, a much richer, more coguitively adventurous and social interactionist conceptualization of academic writing does emerge in A WG~as students are led from descriptive to analytical discourse, and finally to confidently "creating their own research space." While "write-to-learn" advocates might argue that A WG primarily emphasizes social "positioning" and "display" (two terms used repeatedly in A WG), Swales and Feak seem to assume that graduate students will learn the knowledge-transforming habits of mind that coguitivists value through disciplinary immersion and apprenticeship with graduate faculty mentors. It is on the more social side of negotiating academic discourse that we who focus on rhetoric and language are equipped to be facilitative (see A WG, p. 3), and it is on the basis of this insight that Swales and Feak help us and our students in the succeeding chapters of A WG. In Chapters 2-4, Swales and Feak introduce major "subtasks" underlying academic discourse--general-to-specific movement, problem/solution structure, and data commentary. Each of these chapters, as well as all other chapters in A WG, offer cycles of rhetorical information, discussion of related language issues, and exercises. The opening of Chapter 3, where problem/solution texts are presented as opportunities for students to "position" themselves as "questioning and perceptive" researchers, is a good example of the way Swales and Feak flame their chapters. Usage issues covered in the "language focus" sections are also presented from a functional/rhetorical perspective. For instance, indirect questions are discussed in Chapter 3 as a means of "problema- tizing" previous research. Most noteworthy in the treatment of both linguistic and rhetorical issues is the extent to which the implied user of A WG is conceived of as an intelligent adult flee to make strategic choices. In keeping with this ethic, Swales and Feak's tone throughout is more advisory and tenta- tive than prescriptive. Frequent references to research on academic discourse reveal that while much is known, much remains to be discovered, and that academic writing itself is a vibrant, respectable research area of value and likely interest to students, who are repeatedly invited to examine the discourse of their own fields. Perhaps the task most indicative of Swales and Feak's eagerness to nurture burgeoning professionalism and critical independence is an exercise that asks readers to do something that, as Swales and Feak remark in the Comme~#a~3,, students do all the time, but usually without encouragement from writing textbooks: evaluate as "reasonable" or "unreasonable" an instructor's

Reviews 1 7 7 response to student writing, in this case a "data commentary" (A WG: 9995). While this particular exercise is especially notable for the subtext it presents students who will continue to learn to write in their own fields through evalu- ation of faculty and peer feedback, it is a fairly typical token of the care and thought that Swales and Feak have given to the construction of tasks and explanations throughout their text. With Chapters 5 and 6, on summarizing and critiquing, the focus of A WG shifts to writing with sources. Most striking once again is Swales and Feak's recognition of the basic intelligence of graduate students. Thus, A WG does not assume that faculty expectations are sufficient motivation for graduate students, but rather that they will want to learn to write summary/paraphrases and critiques for more personally and publicly rewarding reasons--as oppor- tunities to demonstrate understanding of their source materials and their field's standards. As with every text type they present, Swales and Feak are reflesh- ingly straightforward in their account of how summaries and critiques are used in the real academic world. They point out, for example, how authors imply their attitudes about a source through the choice of reporting verbs. Swales and Feak admit, too, that critiques are not equally popular in all fields. Further, what we in Western academia consider inappropriate source text use, a.k.a. plagiarism, is presented as a North American/Western European cultural construct, and students are prompted to make cross-cultural comparisons. Chapters 7 and 8, on constructing the research paper (RP), are the central chapters of A WG, since all graduate writing and study should culminate in the ability to make an original contribution to one's field in a published RP. Students intimidated by the RP should be comforted by the realization that, as Swales and Feak point out, all the preceding chapters of A WG have prepared them to write the RP, since what they have learned in each case figures in its construction. But teachers may be more impressed by Swales and Feak's efforts to raise the rhetor- ical consciousness of students who tend to underestimate the RP writing task, viewing it as a simple, transparent report of procedures and findings. The rhetor- ical nature of the RP is fully treated in these chapters, as in Swales and Feak's demonstration in an apparently "objective" aerospace RP of authorial "presence," to use Harvey's (1994) term for writer engagement and control. Even some teach- ers may be surprised to learn how much room for rhetorical maneuvering there is in the RP. Swales and Feak's advice on "creating a research space" in the report Introduction, however, will not be news to teachers already familiar with Swates' earlier research (e.g., 1990). But for students unaccustomed to rhetorical reading of the RP, many of Swales and Feak's observations may come as revelations. It is difficult to imagine students (or teachers) missing the message that pervades all of the authors' counsel on RP writing--that research does not speak for itself; it speaks for, and because of, the researcher (cf., Keller 1985). Several questions may arise, however, in the minds of both students and teachers using the last few chapters of A WG. Students and teachers may question Swales and Feak's decision to employ a mini-RP that they themselves composed to illustrate each RP section. A greater number and variety of sample RP texts would seem to be desirable. Some teachers may also question the

1 78 Reviews wisdom of encouraging novices to begin the RP at the Methods section [although other ESP specialists besides Swales and Feak, e.g., Jacoby, Leech and Holten (1995), do encourage the "Methods first" composing sequence]. A more general problem for teachers is whether students in the early stages of graduate school will have done any research that they can write up. Might not an extended literature review, a genre not covered in A WG, be a more useful and doable exercise for them, or perhaps a formal research proposal? Yet another question is how helpful the RP chapters will be to students in fields such as history, economics, journalism, and other disciplines in which experi- mental research is less popular. To be fair, A WG does not claim to address the needs of all graduate students in all fields. No matter what textbook is used in a research writing course for graduate students, teachers should expect to deviate from and supplement it, as the Commentary recommends, and most of all to "negotiate the syllabus" (Frodesen 1995) with their students. What comes across perhaps most clearly throughout A WG is the fact that it has emerged from the authors' own work with graduate students, whom they genuinely admire and enjoy teaching. Swales and Feak's intimate acquaintance with the needs and talents of graduate students is abundantly evident not just in the text proper, but also in the appendices of A WG, where the authors dispense advice on the vagaries of article use across disciplines, the Western academic penchant for Latin phrases, and the unwritten rules of academic e- mail etiquette. Swales and Feak's sensitivity to students' needs is equally evident in the Commentary, where they freely defer to their own students' observations on academic literacy practices, and worry over proper pacing of lessons for quick-witted graduate students. Indeed, what is most impressive overall about A WG and the Comnzentary is the respect shown for the intelli- gence of both students and their writing teachers. Swales and Feak assume that teachers who use their text will be knowledgeable enough to adapt it to their own purposes and will have the intellectual curiosity and initiative to investi- gate writing across the curriculum along with their students. Even more to the point, the authors assume that armed with the linguistic and rhetorical consciousness that A WG and their teachers can bring them, students will be capable of the strategic choices needed to strike the delicate balance of individ- ual assertion and community membership that is such a vital element of academic writing in English. While one might wish that an even broader range of academic text types and styles were presented in A WG, it would be difficult to find a writing textbook that provides a more expansive view of the universe of academic discourse than A WG does, or that expresses more confidence in the ability of students to become contributors to it. UNDERSTANDING SCIENTIFIC PROSE. Jack Selzer (Ed.). Madison, WI: University of Wisconsin Press, 1993, xv + 388 pp. Reviewed by Ellen Valle The title of this book is a deliberate echo of Brooks and Warren's 1938 classic, Understanding Poetry. Where the earlier book was an attempt to domes- ticate the methods of New Criticism in the analysis of literary texts, the aim of the present work is to demonstrate the practical application of the New Rhetoric to the analysis of scientific writing. A brief introduction by the editor is followed by thirteen essays by various writers, analyzing a single scientific text--an article on evolutionary theory by Stephen Jay Gould and Richard C. Lewontin entitled "The Spandrels of San Marco and the Panglossian Paradigm: A Critique of the Adaptationist Programme". The article was originally published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society of London in 1979, as part of a scientific symposium on evolutionary theory.
